More important than their identities is their role of confirming God’s message by the testimony of “two or three witnesses” (see [Deut 17:6](Deut.17.6)). God provides a twofold witness to the world about the impending judgment, making it clear that his word is certain to be fulfilled ([Deut 19:15](Deut.19.15); [Matt 18:15-16](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.16)).

The instructions to **measure the Temple** are reminiscent of Ezekiel’s visions (see [Ezek 40–42](Ezek.40.1-Ezek.42.20); [43:13-17](Ezek.43.13-Ezek.43.17)). The Jerusalem Temple was destroyed by the Romans in AD 70; these details symbolize God’s precise knowledge of and care for his people who belong to him (cp. [Rev 7:2-4](Rev.7.2-Rev.7.4); [Zech 2:1-5](Zech.2.1-Zech.2.5)).

**The outer courtyard** in the Jerusalem Temple, outside the stone warning fence, was regarded as the place for the Gentile **nations**. John makes a clear distinction between the people God recognizes and those he does not.

The **42 months** and **1,260 days** refer to a period of three and a half years, or a broken seven (see study notes on Dan 7:24-25; 8:26; 9:24-27). John repeatedly uses these time designations in Revelation when persecution is evident and evil appears to dominate the world. God’s people will be secure in him (see study note on Rev 11:1) even though God allows evil forces to persecute them (see [13:7](Rev.13.7); [Mark 10:30](Mark.10.30)).

During the period of persecution, God will not abandon the world but will send his **two witnesses** to proclaim the coming judgment, just as God sent Jonah to Nineveh ([Jon 1:2](Jonah.1.2); [4:11](Jonah.4.11)).
Clothing made of **burlap** was symbolic of mourning or repentance (see [Gen 37:34](Gen.37.34); [2 Sam 3:31](2Sam.3.31); [Neh 9:1](Neh.9.1); [Esth 4:1](Esth.4.1); [Jon 3:6](Jonah.3.6)).
**two olive trees and . . . two lampstands:** See study note on 1:12; see also [Exod 25:31-40](Exod.25.31-Exod.25.40); [Zech 4:2-6](Zech.4.2-Zech.4.6).

In one of the psalms, God is portrayed with **fire** coming from his mouth, a picture of judgment on his enemies ([Ps 18:8](Ps.18.8); see also [2 Sam 22:9](2Sam.22.9)). Cp. Elijah, [2 Kgs 1:1-15](2Kgs.1.1-2Kgs.1.15).

These two witnesses were given **power** to stop the **rain** and bring down plagues, as were Elijah (see [1 Kgs 17:1](1Kgs.17.1); [18:41-46](1Kgs.18.41-1Kgs.18.46)) and Moses (see [Exod 7:14-24](Exod.7.14-Exod.7.24); [8:1–11:10](Exod.8.1-Exod.11.10)).

When the witnesses finish **their testimony***,* the scene changes dramatically. **The beast** (cp. [13:1](Rev.13.1)) is introduced for the first time; it is associated with **the bottomless pit**. Like all enemies of God, the beast engages in **war** against God’s witnesses, and he kills them.
**their bodies will lie in the main street:** Evil is so vindictive that it even desecrates the dead.

**Jerusalem** (literally *the great city*): The designation “the great city” would have immediately suggested Rome to early readers ([16:19](Rev.16.19); [17:18](Rev.17.18); [18:10](Rev.18.10), [16](Rev.18.16), [18-19](Rev.18.18-Rev.18.19), [21](Rev.18.21)). But John also describes it as the city **where their Lord was crucified** as well as **Sodom** and **Egypt**—all places that were hostile to God and his people (see also [17:5](Rev.17.5), [9](Rev.17.9)).
**where their Lord was crucified:** There is a direct connection between how the Lord was treated by evil forces and the experience of persecuted Christians (see [Acts 9:5](Acts.9.5)).
Leaving people’s **bodies** out for public display was a way to dishonor them after their death (see [1 Sam 31:10](1Sam.31.10); the usual Roman custom was to leave bodies hanging after crucifixion).
**peoples, tribes, languages, and nations:** All the peoples of the world are represented in this exhibition.
**All the people . . . will gloat** and **celebrate:** God’s enemies despise and reject his messengers.

The death of the two witnesses is not the end of their ministry. God was not defeated in the death of Jesus and he will not be defeated in the slaughter of his witnesses. The God of the resurrection **breathed life** into the dead so that they **stood up** (see [Ezek 37:3-5](Ezek.37.3-Ezek.37.5), [10](Ezek.37.10)), leaving no doubt about God’s power.
**Terror struck:** It is a fearful experience for sinful humans to face the power of the living God (see [Heb 10:31](Heb.10.31)).
**they rose to heaven in a cloud:** The event is reminiscent of the ascent of Jesus (see [Acts 1:9](Acts.1.9)) and others (see [2 Kgs 2:11-12](2Kgs.2.11-2Kgs.2.12); [1 Thes 4:17](1Thess.4.17)).
An **earthquake** often accompanies key moments in biblical history (see [Exod 19:18](Exod.19.18); [1 Kgs 19:11-12](1Kgs.19.11-1Kgs.19.12); [Matt 27:51](Matt.27.51)).
**Seven thousand:** The number who **died** shows God’s involvement in judgment (contrast [1 Kgs 19:18](1Kgs.19.18)).

**everyone else . . . gave glory to the God of heaven:** Those who survived the earthquake were forced to acknowledge God’s power and sovereignty over the world (see [Phil 2:9-11](Phil.2.9-Phil.2.11)).

The **seventh** trumpet (“the third terror,” [11:14](Rev.11.14); see also [9:12](Rev.9.12)) presents a scene of final judgment and the eternal Kingdom. As in [7:9-17](Rev.7.9-Rev.7.17), this scene provides a dramatic window into the ultimate Christian hope with God. In the midst of a picture of judgment, the reader is reminded of eternity with God.
**Loud voices** in the court of **heaven** sing a victory hymn; the earth has been transformed into the realm of **our Lord** and **his Christ***,* who is enthroned as king **forever**.

**The twenty-four** **elders***,* representing the people of God, confirm God’s victorious enthronement (see study note on 4:4). Their worship acknowledges God’s sovereign rule as **the Almighty** (see [4:10-11](Rev.4.10-Rev.4.11); [5:8-10](Rev.5.8-Rev.5.10)).

The thanksgiving prayer describes God as **the one who is and who always was***;* the description “is still to come” (see [1:4](Rev.1.4), [8](Rev.1.8)) no longer applies, because in this scene eternity has come and God has **begun to reign**.

**The nations were filled with wrath** when they refused to do as God commanded (see [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)). But things will **now** be different because God’s **wrath has come**. God will **reward** his **holy people** (see [Rev 22:12](Rev.22.12)) with new life as his children (see [John 1:12](John.1.12); [20:31](John.20.31)).
**fear your name:** God’s name implies his nature; fearing God’s name means accepting who he is (see “Fear of the Lord” Theme Note).

The end of the age will be the **time to destroy** those who have not accepted God’s love (see [John 3:16-20](John.3.16-John.3.20)). They will go into the lake of fire ([Rev 20:15](Rev.20.15)). This doom of God’s enemies is the third and final terror ([11:14](Rev.11.14)).
This verse provides a dramatic conclusion to the first half of Revelation and a link to the second half.
In this scene, the **Temple** and the **Ark** are symbols of God’s presence; the earthly Ark was the copy of the design of the Ark in heaven (see [Exod 25:40](Exod.25.40); [Heb 8:5](Heb.8.5)).

The people of God, portrayed as a woman who brings forth the Messiah, are under attack by the devil even though he has already been defeated ([12:1-17](Rev.12.1-Rev.12.17)). With his two minions, the beast and the false prophet, Satan attempts to continue controlling the world ([13:1-18](Rev.13.1-Rev.13.18)) before the final confrontation with the Lord ([14:1-20](Rev.14.1-Rev.14.20)).

Satan (pictured as a dragon) plots to challenge God’s purposes but is thwarted. Having failed in direct confrontation with God and Christ, he attempts to attack God’s people. Three brief scenes present an overview of the story ([12:1-6](Rev.12.1-Rev.12.6)), followed by elaborations of the war in heaven ([12:7-9](Rev.12.7-Rev.12.9)) and the war on earth ([12:13-17](Rev.12.13-Rev.12.17)).

The number **twelve** suggests that the **woman** represents God’s people (cp. [12:15-17](Rev.12.15-Rev.12.17); see [Jer 2:32](Jer.2.32); [2 Cor 11:2](2Cor.11.2); [Eph 5:32](Eph.5.32)), from whom came the Messiah. This woman is marked by God’s glory in contrast with the prostitute (see [Rev 17:1-6](Rev.17.1-Rev.17.6)), who is destined for destruction.

The symbolic woman going through the **agony** of **labor** portrays Christ’s birth, reflecting the biblical theme of Israel’s trauma while waiting to be delivered (see [Isa 26:16-18](Isa.26.16-Isa.26.18); [Jer 4:31](Jer.4.31); [Mic 4:9-10](Mic.4.9-Mic.4.10); [John 16:21](John.16.21)).
The **large red dragon** represents Satan (see [12:9](Rev.12.9)).
**seven heads and ten horns:** The numbers represent a mixture of divine and created powers (see [17:7-14](Rev.17.7-Rev.17.14)).
The historic battle between evil and the people of God is staged in cosmic dimensions (see [Gen 3:1-7](Gen.3.1-Gen.3.7), [14-15](Gen.3.14-Gen.3.15); [Job 1:9-12](Job.1.9-Job.1.12)).
Herod’s desire to kill Jesus embodied Satan’s attempt **to devour her baby** after **it was born** (see [Matt 2:7-8](Matt.2.7-Matt.2.8), [16](Matt.2.16)).
Jesus was the **son who was to rule all nations** (see [Luke 1:31-33](Luke.1.31-Luke.1.33); [2:30-32](Luke.2.30-Luke.2.32); cp. [Ps 2:6-12](Ps.2.6-Ps.2.12)).

Although Jesus was killed by agents of the devil, he was **snatched away from the dragon** and raised from the dead ([Matt 28:6](Matt.28.6); [Mark 10:33-34](Mark.10.33-Mark.10.34); [16:6](Mark.16.6); [1 Cor 15:3-4](1Cor.15.3-1Cor.15.4)). Jesus’ entire life on earth, from his birth to his death and resurrection, is compressed into this scene.
**caught up to God and to his throne:** See [Acts 1:9-11](Acts.1.9-Acts.1.11).

Like the people of Israel who were spiritually refined in **the wilderness** (see [Hos 2:14-15](Hos.2.14-Hos.2.15); [Acts 7:38-45](Acts.7.38-Acts.7.45)) and in exile (see [Isa 5:13](Isa.5.13); [Ezek 12:1-3](Ezek.12.1-Ezek.12.3)), the Christian church must face its own wilderness. Revelation presents messages of endurance and perseverance in the face of trouble and shows that God provides places of refuge and avenues of escape for his people (cp. [1 Cor 10:13](1Cor.10.13)). **1,260 days:** See study note on Rev 11:2-3.
This scene clarifies the dragon’s identity and power.

God dispatches **Michael***,* the warrior archangel (see [Dan 12:1](Dan.12.1); [Jude 1:9](Jude.1.9)), to confront **the dragon and his angels**. God does not have to engage in the battle himself (see [Matt 26:53](Matt.26.53)), and Satan is defeated.
Satan’s defeat is encouraging for Christians who, like the recipients of Revelation, are not **afraid to die** (see [John 12:24-26](John.12.24-John.12.26)).
**When the dragon realized:** The scene picks up from [12:9](Rev.12.9).

**two wings . . . of a great eagle** (see [Exod 19:4-6](Exod.19.4-Exod.19.6); [Deut 32:10-11](Deut.32.10-Deut.32.11); [Isa 40:29-31](Isa.40.29-Isa.40.31)): God strengthens his people; he does not promise that they will escape persecution or death.
**a time, times, and half a time:** Usually understood as three and a half years (see [Rev 11:2-3](Rev.11.2-Rev.11.3)).

John pictures Satan as Leviathan (cp. [Job 41:1](Job.41.1)) trying to destroy God’s people (the woman; see study note on Rev 12:1). The protective **earth** responds and the waters of chaos are contained, as at creation (cp. [Gen 1:2](Gen.1.2), [6-7](Gen.1.6-Gen.1.7), [9-10](Gen.1.9-Gen.1.10)).
John portrays the dragon conducting its war ([12:17](Rev.12.17)) through two beasts who with Satan form an evil trinity.
The **dragon** turns his hostility against the woman’s **children** (believers) who **keep God’s commandments** and continue in **their testimony for Jesus**.
**on the shore beside the sea:** By contrast, the Lamb stands on the rock of Zion ([14:1](Rev.14.1)).
The first beast is the second member of the evil trinity (see study note on 12:18–13:18) and should probably be identified with Roman power (see “Four World Empires” Theme Note).

The **beast** emerges from **the sea** (symbolizing evil). Like the dragon, it has **seven heads and** **ten horns** (see [12:3](Rev.12.3)). The **crowns** represent its political and military power (cp. [17:3](Rev.17.3), [7-11](Rev.17.7-Rev.17.11); [Dan 7:7](Dan.7.7), [19-20](Dan.7.19-Dan.7.20)) and indicate that Satan is the head of this beast’s empire.
Satan makes the beast a pseudo-deity by giving it his **power***,* **throne***,* and **authority**. In the first century, Roman emperors increasingly claimed divinity.
Satan often imitates God. Here **the beast** mimics the death and resurrection of Jesus.

That **one of the heads** had been fatally **wounded** but **was healed** has led to its identification with Nero. A tradition emerged that the emperor Nero (AD 54–68) was so evil that he either did not really die or would be reincarnated as another tyrant like Domitian (AD 81–96). In [17:9-10](Rev.17.9-Rev.17.10), the beast’s seven heads are linked both to *seven hills* (Rome) and to *seven kings.*

The four characteristics of **the beast** are that he (1) blasphemes God, (2) has **authority** for a limited time, (3) makes **war** against God’s people, and (4) rules the world. But God is in control.
The **forty-two months** are the three and a half years of persecution and evil domination (see study note on 11:2-3).
The beast’s **authority** extends over all the **people** of the world.
Those who **worshiped the beast** receive its mark ([13:15-17](Rev.13.15-Rev.13.17)) and are not listed in the **Book of Life** (see [20:12](Rev.20.12)).

The scene ([13:1-10](Rev.13.1-Rev.13.10)) ends with a dramatic conclusion patterned on [Jer 15:2](Jer.15.2); [43:11](Jer.43.11). **Anyone with ears to hear** must pay attention, because judgment is coming (cp. [Rev 2:7](Rev.2.7), [11](Rev.2.11), [17](Rev.2.17)).
**God’s holy people** are summoned to **endure** and **remain faithful** while experiencing temporary **persecution**.

**another beast:** This second beast, the third member of the evil trinity (see study note on 12:18–13:18), is later called the “false prophet” ([16:13](Rev.16.13)). As a high priest of false religion, he leads the world into worshiping the first beast and the dragon (see also [16:13-14](Rev.16.13-Rev.16.14)).

The **beast** is portrayed as **a lamb***,* the same symbol used to represent Christ (see [5:6-13](Rev.5.6-Rev.5.13); [7:9-17](Rev.7.9-Rev.7.17); [14:1-4](Rev.14.1-Rev.14.4)), but this lamb **spoke** like **a dragon**. The image is of a fraudulent messiah.
The **two horns** might stand for two emperors, perhaps Nero and Domitian.
The second beast derives its power from **the first beast**, which in turn answers to the dragon ([13:4](Rev.13.4)).
**he required . . . people to worship the first beast:** Imperial Rome demanded worship of the emperor Domitian.

**whose fatal wound had been healed:** This description might refer to Domitian, who was viewed as the reincarnation of Nero (see study note on 13:3). The image is a picture of the constant reemergence of evil, particularly in the latter days (see study note on 17:8).

In New Testament times, false prophets astounded people with reports of divine visitations and of idols speaking for the gods they represented (see [Acts 16:16-18](Acts.16.16-Acts.16.18); [1 Cor 12:2-3](1Cor.12.2-1Cor.12.3)). Such practices involved worship of demons (see [1 Cor 10:20-21](1Cor.10.20-1Cor.10.21)) and were epitomized in the Roman emperor cult. Those who refused to conform were put to death.
**he was allowed. . . . He was then permitted:** God never relinquishes ultimate authority. These creatures of evil have been allowed to rebel against God, but they are not in control.

**small and great, rich and poor, free and slave:** All humanity is required to accept the beast’s evil **mark** of ownership (see [14:9](Rev.14.9), [11](Rev.14.11); [19:20](Rev.19.20); [20:4](Rev.20.4)), a precondition for all commerce (the right to **buy or sell**). The text does not explicitly tell us what the mark is or looks like.
**On the right hand or on the forehead** suggests the branding of slaves—the beast owns them.
**the number representing his name:** In both Hebrew and Greek, letters of the alphabet represent numbers, which gave names a numerical value ([13:18](Rev.13.18)).
**Wisdom is needed:** John is giving a clue to help his readers **solve the meaning** of the beast’s **number**.
**of a man:** John hides the man’s identity, perhaps because revealing the name would place him and his readers in danger (cp. use of Babylon as a symbol for Rome, [17:9](Rev.17.9)).

The number **666** represents supernatural evil (see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note). John might have used the transliteration *Caesar Neron* (a Hebrew spelling of the name) to arrive at the number 666. Later scribes, who spoke Greek but not Hebrew, corrected the number to *616* in some manuscripts, probably to match the name’s numerical value in Greek.
The true **Lamb** and his followers starkly contrast with the evil trinity.
**standing:** See [5:6](Rev.5.6); study note on 12:18.
**144,000:** God’s righteous remnant (see study note on 7:4-8).

The brand on **their foreheads** (contrast [13:16-17](Rev.13.16-Rev.13.17)) is the **name** of both **the Lamb** and **his Father***,* reflecting the union of Jesus and the Father (see [John 5:20-23](John.5.20-John.5.23); [14:5-10](John.14.5-John.14.10); [17:22](John.17.22)).

**This great choir sang a** . . . **new song** that only those **who had been redeemed from the earth** could **learn**. These people had died and were already with the Lord, which might explain why John did not include the content of their refrain for readers still in the battle of life (cp. [2 Cor 12:4](2Cor.12.4)).
These warriors were ritually **pure** (unpolluted) and morally **without blame**.

**They have kept themselves as pure as virgins:** Referring to men as *virgins* is a metaphor for the faithfulness of God’s people. The image might refer to the church as the virgin bride of Christ (see [2 Cor 11:2](2Cor.11.2); [Eph 5:25-27](Eph.5.25-Eph.5.27)); it also suggests that the church constitutes soldiers in a holy war that are required to keep themselves chaste (see [Deut 23:9-10](Deut.23.9-Deut.23.10); [1 Sam 21:5](1Sam.21.5)).

These faithful people are **a special offering** (literally *firstfruits;* see [Exod 13:14-16](Exod.13.14-Exod.13.16); [23:19](Exod.23.19); [Lev 23:9-14](Lev.23.9-Lev.23.14); [Num 3:40-51](Num.3.40-Num.3.51); [18:15-20](Num.18.15-Num.18.20); [Luke 2:22-24](Luke.2.22-Luke.2.24)) who **have been purchased** for God.

**They have told no lies:** John teaches that liars will never enter heaven ([Rev 21:8](Rev.21.8), [27](Rev.21.27); [22:15](Rev.22.15); see also [John 8:44](John.8.44)). The followers of Jesus speak and live the truth (see also [John 8:32](John.8.32); [14:6](John.14.6)).
Three angels are **flying through the sky** with messages from God.
The first **angel** proclaims **the eternal Good News***,* which includes the message that God **will sit as judge**—the end is near, so this message provides a last-chance summons to repentance.

**Babylon** is probably a cryptic designation for Rome (see [16:19](Rev.16.19); [17:5-9](Rev.17.5-Rev.17.9)); it represents earthly power and corruption. The coming of God as judge ([14:7](Rev.14.7)) includes the end of earthly powers.

The **third angel** announces God’s judgment ([14:7](Rev.14.7)) on the counterfeit worship of the **beast and** **his statue** (see [13:12-18](Rev.13.12-Rev.13.18); [19:20](Rev.19.20); [20:4](Rev.20.4)). God’s response to the rebellion against his reign is **anger** or **wrath***,* pictured as a **cup** of bitter **wine** (see ch [16](Rev.16.1-Rev.16.21); [19:15](Rev.19.15)).

**fire and burning sulfur . . . smoke:** This description of judgment (see also [19:20](Rev.19.20); [20:10](Rev.20.10), [14-15](Rev.20.14-Rev.20.15)) echoes God’s judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah ([Gen 18:16–19:28](Gen.18.16-Gen.19.28)).
Those condemned to a fiery end will suffer **in the presence of the holy angels and the Lamb** (cp. [Luke 16:22-24](Luke.16.22-Luke.16.24)).

The threat of **persecution** and death was very real to the Christians first reading this letter, so John calls God’s people to obedience and faithfulness (see [2:10](Rev.2.10); [3:10](Rev.3.10); [12:17](Rev.12.17); [13:10](Rev.13.10)).
A dramatic **voice from heaven** once again instructs John to **write** (see [1:11](Rev.1.11), [19](Rev.1.19); [21:5](Rev.21.5); cp. [10:4](Rev.10.4)).
**Blessed are those who die in the Lord:** God desires that those who endure persecution be with him and enjoy his blessings and **rest**.
The mention of **hard work** and **good deeds** in connection with eternal reward foreshadows the assigning of rewards based on works ([20:12](Rev.20.12)).
Two brief scenes portray God’s judgment.
**the Son of Man:** Or *like a son of man;* see study note on 1:13.
A **gold crown** is a symbol of status or power, clearly distinguishing Jesus from the angels (see [4:4](Rev.4.4); [6:2](Rev.6.2); [9:7](Rev.9.7); [12:3](Rev.12.3); [13:1](Rev.13.1)).
The **sharp sickle** is symbolic of God’s harvest of judgment (see [14:17-18](Rev.14.17-Rev.14.18); see also [Jer 51:33](Jer.51.33); [Hos 6:11](Hos.6.11); [Mic 4:12-13](Mic.4.12-Mic.4.13)).
The **Temple** and the **altar** represent God’s presence (see [9:13](Rev.9.13); [11:19](Rev.11.19); [16:7](Rev.16.7)).
The **ripe** *. . .* **grapes** (see [Amos 8:2](Amos.8.2)) that are **trampled in the winepress** emphasize God’s power to judge (see [Rev 19:15](Rev.19.15); [Joel 3:13](Joel.3.13)).

Winepresses were built outside cities and towns; here, **the city** is Jerusalem. The bloody river of death stretched about **180 miles.** God’s enemies stand no chance when the Son of Man comes in judgment. The carnage here is closely linked with the final battle in [Rev 19:17-21](Rev.19.17-Rev.19.21); God is just and fair in giving people exactly what they deserve (see [16:5-7](Rev.16.5-Rev.16.7)).

The third and final cycle of seven judgments (see study note on 6:1–16:21) is introduced with a vision of God’s victorious people singing a hymn of praise ([15:2-4](Rev.15.2-Rev.15.4)). Then a scene of the Temple is presented ([15:5-8](Rev.15.5-Rev.15.8)), from which angels emerge bearing the bowls of God’s judgment upon the earth ([16:1-21](Rev.16.1-Rev.16.21)).

This cycle of **seven last plagues** ([15:1–16:21](Rev.15.1-Rev.16.21)) brings **God’s wrath** against his enemies **to completion** (see [16:17](Rev.16.17); [Amos 1–2](Amos.1.1-Amos.2.16); [Rom 1:18–2:16](Rom.1.18-Rom.2.16)). Revelation returns later to the subjects of God’s wrath ([Rev 19:15-21](Rev.19.15-Rev.19.21)).

The **glass sea mixed with fire** symbolizes victory through testing. Those **who had been victorious over the beast** (see [13:1-8](Rev.13.1-Rev.13.8), [15-18](Rev.13.15-Rev.13.18)) hold **harps** that represent ultimate peace. Their place **on** the *glass sea* (cp. [4:6](Rev.4.6)) symbolizes their endurance in the *fire* of persecution (cp. [Ps 66:12](Ps.66.12); [Isa 43:2](Isa.43.2); [Dan 3:8-30](Dan.3.8-Dan.3.30)).
The **song of Moses** and **the Lamb** signifies that God’s will is united in the old and new covenants.

The **Lord God, the** **Almighty** (see also [1:8](Rev.1.8); [4:8](Rev.4.8); [11:17](Rev.11.17); [16:7](Rev.16.7); [19:6](Rev.19.6); [21:22](Rev.21.22)): For persecuted Christians, the message that God is all-powerful provides great comfort and security.
The truth that God is also **just and true** is the foundation of human integrity in the midst of a confused, unjust, and dishonest world.
God is the supreme, universal **King of the nations***,* not a localized deity attached to one nation or to a human monarch with limited authority.

**Who will not fear** . . . **and glorify your name?** This rhetorical question (cp. [Jer 10:7](Jer.10.7)) assumes that only a fool would fail to do so (cp. [Rev 14:7](Rev.14.7); [16:9](Rev.16.9); see [Pss 14:1](Ps.14.1); [53:1](Ps.53.1)).
God **alone** is **holy:** See [Rev 16:5](Rev.16.5); [Lev 11:44](Lev.11.44); [1 Pet 1:16](1Pet.1.16). God’s holiness is the basis for our worship and salvation.

**All nations will . . . worship:** Some will be forced to acknowledge God (cp. [Phil 2:10-11](Phil.2.10-Phil.2.11)), but all will recognize that God’s **deeds** and judgments **have been revealed** and are **righteous** and just.

**God’s Tabernacle** implies God’s presence (see [John 1:14](John.1.14)); even the plagues have their source in God’s presence. Christ’s sacrifice ([Matt 27:51](Matt.27.51); [Mark 15:38](Mark.15.38); [Heb 6:19-20](Heb.6.19-Heb.6.20); [10:19-20](Heb.10.19-Heb.10.20)) removed the veil between God and humanity (see [Exod 26:31-35](Exod.26.31-Exod.26.35); [Lev 16](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.34)). Now those who do not belong to Christ experience the full force of God’s presence (see [Rev 20:11-15](Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15); [Isa 13:4-12](Isa.13.4-Isa.13.12); [Zeph 2:1-3](Zeph.2.1-Zeph.2.3); [Mal 3:2-3](Mal.3.2-Mal.3.3)).

**white linen:** Linen, a symbol of purity, was also worn by the priests when performing their duties (see [Exod 28:39-43](Exod.28.39-Exod.28.43); [Lev 16:4](Lev.16.4), [23](Lev.16.23); see also [Ezek 9:2-3](Ezek.9.2-Ezek.9.3); [Dan 12:6-7](Dan.12.6-Dan.12.7)). The function of these angels is not intercession; they are agents of judgment. The linen therefore represents the purity and justice of God’s judgment.
The **gold sashes across their chests** probably symbolize their divine mission as ministers of justice on God’s behalf (cp. [Rev 1:13](Rev.1.13)).
**the four living beings:** See [4:6-8](Rev.4.6-Rev.4.8).
**a gold bowl:** These bowls are probably like the offering pans that were used in ancient worship (see [Exod 37:16](Exod.37.16)).

**The Temple was filled with smoke** as a symbol of **God’s glory and power** ([Isa 6:4](Isa.6.4); see [Exod 19:16-18](Exod.19.16-Exod.19.18); [40:34-35](Exod.40.34-Exod.40.35); [1 Kgs 8:10-13](1Kgs.8.10-1Kgs.8.13)).

These **seven bowls** filled with God’s wrath represent the final judgments on the world; with the seventh bowl, **“It is finished!”** is shouted from God’s throne ([16:17](Rev.16.17); cp. [John 19:30](John.19.30)).
The **mighty voice** probably belongs to God (also in [6:6](Rev.6.6); [9:13](Rev.9.13); [16:17](Rev.16.17); [18:4](Rev.18.4); [19:5](Rev.19.5); see [Isa 66:6](Isa.66.6)).
The **malignant sores** are reminiscent of the sixth plague of Egypt ([Exod 9:9-11](Exod.9.9-Exod.9.11)).

The plagues of the **second** and **third** bowls are similar to the first plague of Egypt ([Exod 7:17-21](Exod.7.17-Exod.7.21)). Perhaps John had in mind that much of Rome’s food and wealth came by sea. After Julius Caesar rid the sea of pirates, shipping became Rome’s lifeblood. Its end would mean economic death for the empire (see [Rev 18:17-19](Rev.18.17-Rev.18.19)).

**the angel who had authority over all water:** Angels and archangels are portrayed as having special roles in the hierarchy of heaven (see [Dan 8:16](Dan.8.16); [9:21](Dan.9.21); [10:13](Dan.10.13), [21](Dan.10.21); [12:1](Dan.12.1); [Luke 1:19](Luke.1.19), [26](Luke.1.26); see also *1 Enoch* 66:1-2). This angel confirms **these judgments** as coming from God, who is both **just** and **holy**.

Punishment of God’s enemies is a **just reward** because they killed God’s **holy people** and **prophets**. Because they have **shed** *. . .* **blood***,* they must **drink** *. . .* **blood**. The principle of *lex talionis* (the law of retribution), the basis of Roman and Jewish jurisprudence, means that God is completely just in judging and rewarding people on the basis of what they have done (see [2:23](Rev.2.23); [11:18](Rev.11.18); [14:13](Rev.14.13); [18:6](Rev.18.6); [20:12](Rev.20.12), [13](Rev.20.13); [22:12](Rev.22.12)).

**I heard a voice from the altar:** The antiphonal response to the angel’s proclamation ([16:5-6](Rev.16.5-Rev.16.6)) affirms God’s authority and justice. This doxology in the midst of judgment reminds persecuted Christians that God truly cares about his suffering servants and fulfills his own purpose in everything.
The **fourth** *. . .* **bowl** is unlike any of the plagues of Egypt or the earlier seals or trumpets.

**Everyone was burned:** Contrast [7:16](Rev.7.16). Yet the recipients of this judgment refused to **repent** or **give** God **glory** (see [9:20-21](Rev.9.20-Rev.9.21); [16:11](Rev.16.11); cp. [14:6-7](Rev.14.6-Rev.14.7)); they even **cursed the name of God**.

**the throne of the beast:** John might be alluding to Rome, the political power of his time. Built on seven hills ([17:9](Rev.17.9)), Rome’s empire spanned the sea ([13:1](Rev.13.1)) and ruled the world ([13:7](Rev.13.7)).
**plunged into darkness:** Similar to the ninth plague of Egypt ([Exod 10:22](Exod.10.22)) and to the fourth trumpet ([Rev 8:12](Rev.8.12)).

**ground their teeth** \[literally *gnawed their tongues*\] . . . **cursed the God of heaven:** Both pain and hostility motivated these responses to punishment (cp. [Matt 8:12](Matt.8.12); [13:42](Matt.13.42), [50](Matt.13.50); [22:13](Matt.22.13); [24:51](Matt.24.51); [25:30](Matt.25.30); [Luke 13:28](Luke.13.28)).

The **Euphrates***,* the largest **river** in Mesopotamia, stood between Babylon and Israel and formed the eastern boundary of the Roman Empire. If it **dried up***,* it would allow **kings from the east** to move their armies westward (cp. [9:13-16](Rev.9.13-Rev.9.16)). From John’s perspective as an ancient Jewish writer, these armies would always be identified with Mesopotamia rather than with countries farther east such as China or India.

Three agents of deceit, **evil spirits** in the form of **frogs***,* represent the **demonic** role of the evil trinity. Although the powers of evil **battle against the Lord***,* it is **God the Almighty***,* not any evil power, who is in control.

Readers are warned to **look** because the Lord will **come as unexpectedly as a thief** (see also [3:3](Rev.3.3); [Matt 24:43](Matt.24.43); [25:13](Matt.25.13); [1 Thes 5:2](1Thess.5.2); [2 Pet 3:10](2Pet.3.10)). Being ready for his coming requires preparation; those who are not prepared will not have the proper **clothing** and will find themselves **naked** (see [Matt 22:11-13](Matt.22.11-Matt.22.13)). This imagery recalls the two failing churches: lifeless Sardis, which is told to “wake up” ([Rev 3:2](Rev.3.2)), and lukewarm Laodicea, which is advised to obtain proper clothing ([3:18](Rev.3.18)).

The name **Armageddon** (or *Harmagedon*) is probably derived from Hebrew *har* (“mountain,” “hill”) plus *Megiddo,* which was one of the three cities fortified by Solomon along with Gezer in the south and Hazor in the north ([1 Kgs 9:15](1Kgs.9.15)). The fortress of Megiddo stood on a hill in the largest pass through the Carmel range, strategically guarding the Jezreel Valley. The city was situated on the Via Maris, the main highway between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Many armies used this route, and the site became known as a bloody battlefield. It was here, for instance, that Pharaoh Neco, on his way to fight the Assyrians, killed Josiah ([2 Kgs 23:29](2Kgs.23.29)). Armageddon thus became a symbolic term epitomizing the final conflict between God and the forces of evil.

When **the seventh** *. . .* **bowl** is poured out, an unexpected event occurs. The enemies of God had assembled themselves for battle, but when the decisive moment arrives, instead of the battle comes the shout, **“It is finished!”** Jesus uttered these same words from the cross when he had finished his work ([John 19:30](John.19.30)). No one can ultimately fight God. Therefore, this scene pictures an end to rebellion against God. What remains are various descriptions of the end.

The catastrophic events of this judgment scene recapitulate the scenes portraying the destruction of the world ([6:12-14](Rev.6.12-Rev.6.14); [11:13](Rev.11.13)). They also foreshadow the final judgment ([20:11-15](Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15)) when the earth will be dismantled to make way for the new creation ([21:1](Rev.21.1); cp. [Isa 45:2](Isa.45.2); [Rom 8:19-22](Rom.8.19-Rom.8.22)).
Despite the severity of these plagues, the people of the world again **cursed God** rather than recognizing his reason for the judgments (see [9:20](Rev.9.20); [16:9](Rev.16.9), [11](Rev.16.11)).
The **terrible hailstorm** is a reminder of the seventh plague on Egypt ([Exod 9:23-24](Exod.9.23-Exod.9.24)).

The great drama in this section focuses on the powers that are hostile to God and responsible for the persecution and suffering of God’s people. Rome’s power was captivating to many ([17:6](Rev.17.6)); John purposely defines Rome’s sins and provides God’s assessment ([17:3-18](Rev.17.3-Rev.17.18)) before outlining its fall ([18:1-24](Rev.18.1-Rev.18.24)) and heaven’s response ([19:1-10](Rev.19.1-Rev.19.10)).

**One of the** *. . .* **angels** of judgment addresses John and summons him to a new scene in which he sees the coming **judgment** of **the great prostitute, who rules over many waters**. Rome, located on the Tiber River, controlled the seats of power and water trade routes throughout the Mediterranean, from the British Isles to the Euphrates River.
**Adultery with her** is a biblical image for serving other gods (see, e.g., [Exod 34:12-16](Exod.34.12-Exod.34.16); [Judg 2:17](Judg.2.17); [Hos 2](Hos.2.1-Hos.2.23)).

**drunk by . . . her immorality:** Drunkenness in Scripture often depicts nations that indulge in wanton and immoral behavior (see [Rev 18:3](Rev.18.3), [9](Rev.18.9); [Jer 25:27](Jer.25.27); [51:7](Jer.51.7); [Lam 4:21](Lam.4.21); [Ezek 23:33](Ezek.23.33)).

John is carried **in the Spirit into the wilderness***,* his way of describing a visionary experience (see [1:10](Rev.1.10); [4:2](Rev.4.2)). He sees a depiction of Rome’s moral corruption and excessive luxury (see [18:12-13](Rev.18.12-Rev.18.13), [16](Rev.18.16)) that illustrates how such wealth can become an abomination to God.
The **beast** here is like the second figure in the evil trinity (see [13:1-4](Rev.13.1-Rev.13.4)).
**blasphemies against God:** See [13:5-6](Rev.13.5-Rev.13.6).
**purple and scarlet:** Clothing in these two colors indicated royalty and carnality, respectively.
**a gold goblet:** See [Jer 51:7](Jer.51.7).

Using code language, John was probably referring to Rome (see [17:9](Rev.17.9)) as **Babylon the Great, Mother of All Prostitutes**. Babylon was a symbol of the idolatries and demonic **obscenities** of the world. As *Mother*, she had produced offspring who copied her character. Rome, like Babylon, prostituted herself to false gods and led other nations into adultery and idolatry.

**God’s holy people** *. . .* **were witnesses for Jesus** to the point of shedding their **blood** (see [16:6](Rev.16.6); [Heb 12:4](Heb.12.4)). In John’s time, Rome was responsible for this persecution.
In response to John’s amazement, **the angel** prepares him to understand the **mystery** ([17:8-14](Rev.17.8-Rev.17.14)).
The destruction within this vision contrasts with the destiny of the people of God in the new heaven and earth (see [21:1-4](Rev.21.1-Rev.21.4)).

**The beast . . . was once alive but isn’t now . . . will soon come up:** When Domitian became emperor (AD 81–96), he was as evil as Nero (both were fierce persecutors of the church), and many thought he was the embodiment of Nero’s spirit, if not Nero himself (perhaps similar to the way that John the Baptist was considered to embody Elijah’s spirit; see [Mal 4:5](Mal.4.5); [Matt 11:14](Matt.11.14); [Luke 1:17](Luke.1.17); [John 1:21](John.1.21)).
**you saw:** The past tense indicates that the angel’s interpretation took place after John’s vision.
**was once alive but isn’t now:** This contrasts with God, “who is, who always was, and who is still to come” ([Rev 1:4](Rev.1.4), [8](Rev.1.8)).
**the bottomless pit:** See study note on 9:1-12.

In contrast to God’s people, the **people** of **this world** are **not written in the Book of Life** (see [20:11-15](Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15)). They **will be amazed** by the apparent resurrection of the beast (see study note on 17:10-11; see also [13:13-17](Rev.13.13-Rev.13.17)).
**The seven heads of the beast represent the seven hills** on which Rome was built (see study note on 16:10-11).

**Five kings have already fallen:** If these kings represent Roman emperors, and the starting point for numbering them is the switch from a republic to an empire with Augustus (29 BC–AD 14), then the fifth in line would be Nero (AD 54–68), **the sixth** would be Vespasian, and **the seventh** would be Titus. **The eighth king** would then be Domitian.
**that was, but is no longer:** Early commentators argued that Domitian was an embodiment of Nero’s spirit (see study note on 17:8).
**like the other seven:** This apparently invincible ruler was also **headed for destruction**.

The **ten horns***,* symbolic of the world kingdoms that follow **the beast***,* rule simultaneously under his direction. While these verses have caused speculation concerning a ten-nation confederacy (from the client kingdoms of Rome, to the states opposed to the Holy Roman Empire, to the European Union), these conjectures are beside the point, which is that all nations opposed to God will be defeated ([17:14](Rev.17.14)).

Whatever power they amass, the beast and ten kings ([17:11-12](Rev.17.11-Rev.17.12)) have no hope of winning because Jesus is **Lord of all lords** (see [19:11-16](Rev.19.11-Rev.19.16)). Those God has **called and chosen** and who remain **faithful** to him will stand **with him** as victors.

While **the prostitute** rules over the **masses***,* it does not bring her victory. Instead, the **beast** hates and kills the great prostitute. Satan strikes even those he uses for his evil purposes.

John provides another reminder that God is in control; God puts **a plan** into the **minds** of the enemy that will fulfill the Lord’s divine **purposes** (e.g., [Exod 7:3](Exod.7.3); [35:31-35](Exod.35.31-Exod.35.35); [Ezra 7:27](Ezra.7.27); [Rom 9:18](Rom.9.18), [21](Rom.9.21)).
This chapter contains seven poetic responses to the fall of Babylon (or Rome; see study note on 17:5).

The angel’s powerful taunt song is the first poetic response. Ancient taunt songs derided a defeated enemy (see [Isa 13:19-22](Isa.13.19-Isa.13.22); [34:10-17](Isa.34.10-Isa.34.17)). In these taunts, the fall of Babylon (or Rome; see study note on Rev 14:8) is portrayed as a traumatic event for subservient kingdoms and especially for those who had profited from her luxury. The sacking of Rome by the Goths and Visigoths (AD 400s) brought the prosperous empire to an end.
This **angel** derived his splendor **from heaven**. The word **splendor** is normally used for the divine presence.

**Babylon is fallen:** See [Isa 21:9](Isa.21.9). Once a beautifully dressed woman (see [Rev 17:4](Rev.17.4)), Babylon (Rome) became a desolate den for **demons** and unclean birds such as vultures (cp. [Isa 13:20-22](Isa.13.20-Isa.13.22); [Jer 4:23-31](Jer.4.23-Jer.4.31); [50:39](Jer.50.39)).
**extravagant luxury:** Rome plundered conquered nations of their wealth before God’s justice fell on her.
This second poetic response (see study note on 18:1-24) is a warning **from heaven** to flee the doomed city.

**Do not take part in her sins:** Association with the evil city could lead to being identified with it in punishment and even involved with it in its sins (see [Gen 13:8-13](Gen.13.8-Gen.13.13); [19:1-29](Gen.19.1-Gen.19.29); cp. [Jer 51:6](Jer.51.6), [45](Jer.51.45)).

**God remembers:** His response may seem slow ([Ps 103:8](Ps.103.8); [145:8](Ps.145.8); [Joel 2:13](Joel.2.13); [Jon 4:2](Jonah.4.2)), but God is not weak, and he does not forget either good or evil ([Rev 16:19](Rev.16.19); [Gen 19:29](Gen.19.29); [1 Sam 1:19](1Sam.1.19)).

**Double her penalty:** The severity of some sins required a double recompense (see [Exod 22:4](Exod.22.4), [7](Exod.22.7), [9](Exod.22.9); cp. [Isa 40:2](Isa.40.2); [Jer 16:18](Jer.16.18); [17:18](Jer.17.18)).
**I am queen:** Cp. [Ezek 28:1-2](Ezek.28.1-Ezek.28.2).

The **plagues** ([18:2-3](Rev.18.2-Rev.18.3)) are a reminder that destruction was not merely a human action; it is the **Lord God who judges her**. He **is mighty***,* able to accomplish what he promises.
These three laments highlight the grief of those who profited most from the wicked city’s rich lifestyle (cp. [Ezek 27](Ezek.27.1-Ezek.27.36)).
The **kings of the world** lament as they **mourn** the loss of the **luxury** they had obtained from alliance with the wicked city.
With a **terrified** sense of separation and abandonment (see [18:15](Rev.18.15), [17](Rev.18.17)), the kings **stand at a distance** in a futile attempt to avoid punishment.

**The merchants of the world** sing the second lament ([18:14](Rev.18.14); see study note on 18:9-19). They profited from the Roman economy ([18:12-13](Rev.18.12-Rev.18.13)), but their trade ceased as the great city was swiftly destroyed.

This cargo list suggests the extent of the wealth Rome pillaged from the rest of its empire (cp. [Ezek 27:12-24](Ezek.27.12-Ezek.27.24)). Some of the most expensive products in the ancient world are mentioned in this indictment of ostentatious materialism and pride.
**bodies:** Rome developed a huge slave market, which some historians have estimated at nearly 20% of the population.
The merchants would lament the fall of Rome (see study note on 18:1-3) because it would **forever** end their accustomed **luxuries**. Material goods can be swept aside **in a single moment**.

**all the captains:** Seafarers sing the third lament (see study note on 18:9-19). Their mourning focuses on the breakdown of communication and transportation. During the reign of Julius Caesar, the Mediterranean was cleared of pirates and trade blossomed under the region’s Roman law enforcement. The swift loss of Roman authority would upset the system of trade.

The laments ([18:9-19](Rev.18.9-Rev.18.19)) stimulate a call for **heaven** to **rejoice**. The **people of God** are not to grieve, because the judgment was for their **sakes***;* they had suffered persecution from the evil forces represented by the great city.
The songs responding to Babylon’s fall ([18:1-24](Rev.18.1-Rev.18.24)) conclude with a portrayal of the city’s doom.

**a boulder the size of a huge millstone:** Heavy millstones, shaped for grinding olives or grain, were used throughout the ancient world. Jesus also spoke of using such stones in judgment (see [Matt 18:6](Matt.18.6)). The dramatically thrown boulder signified that the power of Rome was forever **thrown down**.

This section expands the message of the sixth song of response ([18:20](Rev.18.20); see study note on 18:1-24), which called for rejoicing. Various groups direct praises to the Lord. The praises can be divided into two sections: thankfulness for the destruction of the evildoers ([19:1-4](Rev.19.1-Rev.19.4)) and thankfulness for the reward of God’s people ([19:5-8](Rev.19.5-Rev.19.8)).
This scene focuses on what John **heard** rather than on what he saw. The first three-part praise comes from **a vast crowd** (cp. [7:9-10](Rev.7.9-Rev.7.10)).

**true and just** (see [15:3](Rev.15.3); [16:7](Rev.16.7)): In his righteous justice, God kept his promise of judging **the great prostitute***,* who represents moral and spiritual corruption and persecution of God’s people.
**The smoke from that city:** God’s people praise him once again as they see the evil city’s demise (cp. [14:11](Rev.14.11)).

In response to the first two praises ([19:1-3](Rev.19.1-Rev.19.3)), the **elders** and the **living beings** (see ch [4](Rev.4.1-Rev.4.11)) again prostrate themselves before the enthroned **God** (see [4:10](Rev.4.10); [5:8](Rev.5.8), [14](Rev.5.14); [7:11](Rev.7.11)).
**Amen!** See study note on 5:14.

The focus of the final thunderous **Praise the** **LORD***!* is that God **reigns** as **the Almighty** in complete supremacy (see [1:8](Rev.1.8); [4:8](Rev.4.8); [11:17](Rev.11.17); [15:3](Rev.15.3); [16:7](Rev.16.7), [14](Rev.16.14); [19:15](Rev.19.15); [21:22](Rev.21.22)).

**the wedding feast of the Lamb:** This event—the wedding of the Messiah with his bride, the church (see [Isa 54:5](Isa.54.5); [61:10](Isa.61.10); [Jer 31:32](Jer.31.32); [Ezek 16:7-14](Ezek.16.7-Ezek.16.14); [Hos 2:16-20](Hos.2.16-Hos.2.20); [Mark 2:19-20](Mark.2.19-Mark.2.20); [2 Cor 11:2](2Cor.11.2))—symbolizes complete victory and eternal fellowship.
**finest . . . linen:** See study note on 15:5-6.
**the good deeds of God’s holy people:** See [Eph 2:8-10](Eph.2.8-Eph.2.10); [2 Tim 3:16-17](2Tim.3.16-2Tim.3.17); [Jas 2:18-22](Jas.2.18-Jas.2.22).
**Blessed are those:** This fourth blessing in Revelation (see [1:3](Rev.1.3); [14:13](Rev.14.13); [16:15](Rev.16.15)) affirms the hope of the faithful.
**who are invited:** God is in control and determines who will participate.

**wedding feast** (cp. [19:17](Rev.19.17)): Jesus often used meals to explain the Kingdom ([Matt 22:1-13](Matt.22.1-Matt.22.13); [Luke 14:7-24](Luke.14.7-Luke.14.24)), and he ordained a meal for the church ([Mark 14:22-25](Mark.14.22-Mark.14.25); [1 Cor 11:23-26](1Cor.11.23-1Cor.11.26)).
**These are true words:** This oath asserts the reliability of the message.
The angel issues a stern warning against misdirected worship (cp. [22:8-9](Rev.22.8-Rev.22.9)).

The drama moves into its climactic scenes: God’s enemies are defeated and punished in two episodes ([19:11-21](Rev.19.11-Rev.19.21); [20:7-10](Rev.20.7-Rev.20.10)). Meanwhile, the faithful experience a 1,000-year resurrection ([20:1-6](Rev.20.1-Rev.20.6)) followed by the final judgment ([20:11-15](Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15)).

**Then I saw:** John describes a new vision of Jesus Christ as the holy warrior and conquering King (see [14:1](Rev.14.1); see also [Exod 15:1-7](Exod.15.1-Exod.15.7); [Pss 24:8](Ps.24.8); [78:49-50](Ps.78.49-Ps.78.50); [Isa 59:16-17](Isa.59.16-Isa.59.17)).

The **rider** is both a judge and a **righteous** warrior (see [Isa 11:1-5](Isa.11.1-Isa.11.5)). He is **named Faithful and True:** He embodies God’s authenticity and reliability (see [Rev 19:2](Rev.19.2); [21:5-6](Rev.21.5-Rev.21.6)).
**His eyes were like flames of fire:** See [1:14-16](Rev.1.14-Rev.1.16); [Dan 10:6](Dan.10.6).
Christ, wearing **many crowns***,* is contrasted with the dragon, whose seven heads were each crowned (see [Rev 12:3](Rev.12.3)).

**He wore a robe dipped in blood:** This description may refer to (1) the blood of Christ’s enemies, signifying his total victory ([Isa 63:2-4](Isa.63.2-Isa.63.4)); or (2) Christ’s sacrificial death for humanity ([Rev 1:7](Rev.1.7)).
The **Word of God** is John’s distinctive designation for Jesus (see [John 1:1](John.1.1), [14](John.1.14)).

Christ’s **armies of heaven***,* dressed in victorious **white** and riding **on white horses***,* contrast with the locust forces of the abyss ([9:3-11](Rev.9.3-Rev.9.11)), the three frog-like evil spirits ([16:13](Rev.16.13)), and the defeated armies at Armageddon ([16:16](Rev.16.16); see also [19:19](Rev.19.19)).
**From his mouth . . . a sharp sword:** See [1:16](Rev.1.16); [Heb 4:12](Heb.4.12); see also [Isa 49:2](Isa.49.2); [2 Thes 2:8](2Thess.2.8).
The **iron rod** represents Christ’s power as ruler and as supreme shepherd (see [Pss 2:9](Ps.2.9); [23:4](Ps.23.4)).
His **fierce wrath** will crush his enemies like grapes in **a winepress** ([Isa 63:2-4](Isa.63.2-Isa.63.4)).

**Gather together for the great banquet:** This feast upon **the flesh** of the **armies gathered together to fight against** Christ is contrasted with “the wedding feast of the Lamb” ([19:7](Rev.19.7)). The enemies that form for battle are quickly destroyed ([19:20-21](Rev.19.20-Rev.19.21); see also [14:17-20](Rev.14.17-Rev.14.20); [16:16-21](Rev.16.16-Rev.16.21)). Two feasts—the marriage supper of the Lamb ([19:7-8](Rev.19.7-Rev.19.8)) and the “great supper” of God’s judgment ([19:17-18](Rev.19.17-Rev.19.18), [21](Rev.19.21))—provide two perspectives on the end of time. They illustrate the two sides of the Good News: grace and judgment, reward and punishment (cp. [John 3:16-18](John.3.16-John.3.18)).
**beast . . . false prophet** See [13:1-10](Rev.13.1-Rev.13.10).

The **fiery lake of burning sulfur** provides a picture of eternal punishment (see [20:10](Rev.20.10), [14-15](Rev.20.14-Rev.20.15); [21:8](Rev.21.8); see also [Isa 66:24](Isa.66.24); [Matt 13:41](Matt.13.41), [49-50](Matt.13.49-Matt.13.50); [Mark 9:43](Mark.9.43), [48](Mark.9.48)).

God’s enemies are **thrown** into the *fiery lake.* The two beasts ([Rev 19:20](Rev.19.20)) are followed by the dragon ([20:10](Rev.20.10)) and then by death ([20:14](Rev.20.14)) and unsaved humans ([20:15](Rev.20.15)).

The **entire army** of enemies is dispatched by the **sword** from Christ’s **mouth** (see [1:16](Rev.1.16); [2:12](Rev.2.12), [16](Rev.2.16); see also [Isa 11:4](Isa.11.4); [49:2](Isa.49.2); [2 Thes 2:8](2Thess.2.8)). While one side of God’s word (grace) leads to repentance, the other side (judgment) carries out the death sentence.

There are three parts to this passage: the binding of Satan ([20:1-3](Rev.20.1-Rev.20.3)), the reign of God’s holy people ([20:4-6](Rev.20.4-Rev.20.6)), and the release of Satan for his final attempt at a battle ([20:7-10](Rev.20.7-Rev.20.10)). Four themes emerge: (1) Satan’s war is futile—he cannot withstand even an angel; (2) God’s holy people will be vindicated and glorified; (3) God will have the final victory; and (4) even when sinful and depraved human beings experience Christ’s good purposes in the world, they still flock after Satan when he gains even a small amount of freedom to act.

Like the Old Testament “angel of the LORD” (see [Gen 16:7-11](Gen.16.7-Gen.16.11); [22:15](Gen.22.15); [Exod 3:2](Exod.3.2); [Num 22:22-34](Num.22.22-Num.22.34); [Judg 2:1-4](Judg.2.1-Judg.2.4); [6:11-22](Judg.6.11-Judg.6.22)), the **angel coming down from heaven** has God’s authority, symbolized by the **key** that controls **the bottomless pit** and the power to put **chains** on God’s great enemy (cp. [Rev 12:7-9](Rev.12.7-Rev.12.9)) for **a thousand years.** See “The Thousand Years (The Millennium)” Theme Note.

This incarceration, portrayed as **the bottomless pit***,* is a preliminary defeat for Satan and the powers of evil. Various New Testament passages describe the effect of Christ’s work on Satan ([Luke 10:17-20](Luke.10.17-Luke.10.20); [Acts 10:38](Acts.10.38); [26:18](Acts.26.18); [Rom 16:20](Rom.16.20); [Eph 6:11](Eph.6.11); [Jas 4:7](Jas.4.7); see [Matt 12:24](Matt.12.24); [16:19](Matt.16.19); [18:18](Matt.18.18); [John 12:31](John.12.31); [1 Jn 3:8](1John.3.8)). Christ’s presence with his people binds evil powers (see [2 Thes 2:7](2Thess.2.7)), reminding persecuted Christians that there is a future with God.

**so Satan could not deceive:** Deception is the trademark of the devil, who is a liar (see [John 8:44](John.8.44); [1 Jn 3:8](1John.3.8)); no liar will enter heaven ([Rev 21:8](Rev.21.8), [27](Rev.21.27); [22:15](Rev.22.15)). The faithful believers who experience Christ’s reign will not be deceived.

The **little while** might be the equivalent of the symbolic three and a half years (see [11:2-3](Rev.11.2-Rev.11.3), [9-11](Rev.11.9-Rev.11.11); [12:14](Rev.12.14); [13:5](Rev.13.5))—it is a limited time.

**thrones . . . people sitting on them:** This portrayal of a heavenly tribunal includes the elders ([4:4](Rev.4.4)) on thrones (see [Dan 7:9-10](Dan.7.9-Dan.7.10)), the victorious martyrs (see [Dan 7:22](Dan.7.22)), and all God’s people.
**beheaded for . . . Jesus:** Beheading was a common form of execution for Roman citizens.

The faithful who resisted receiving the **mark** of **the beast** ([Rev 13:16-17](Rev.13.16-Rev.13.17)) will judge the condemned (see [1 Cor 6:2-3](1Cor.6.2-1Cor.6.3)) on thrones similar to those of the worshiping elders (see [Rev 4:10-11](Rev.4.10-Rev.4.11); [5:8-10](Rev.5.8-Rev.5.10); [11:16](Rev.11.16)).
John contrasts **the first resurrection** with **the second death** (see [20:12-15](Rev.20.12-Rev.20.15); cp. [John 5:29](John.5.29)).

**Blessed:** This fifth blessing of Revelation (see also [1:3](Rev.1.3); [14:13](Rev.14.13); [16:15](Rev.16.15); [19:9](Rev.19.9); [22:7](Rev.22.7), [14](Rev.22.14)) focuses on the promised reward of life. God’s faithful people ([20:4](Rev.20.4)) will **reign with** Christ as **priests of God** (see also [1:6](Rev.1.6); [5:10](Rev.5.10)).

Satan’s all-out attempt to conquer God’s people is followed by his fiery demise. This passage has two major purposes: (1) to show God’s absolute justice, because Satan and his followers are worthy of punishment and will never change; and (2) to show the depravity of people who follow Satan. In spite of viewing the nature of Christ’s reign in the world for many years, they still flock to Satan’s standard when he is freed. These factors are the basis for the judgment at the great white throne ([20:11-15](Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15)).

When free to act ([20:7](Rev.20.7)), **Satan** still seeks **to deceive**. He will **gather** a **mighty army** (cp. [Ezek 38–39](Ezek.38.1-Ezek.39.29)) in a final attempt to overwhelm God’s people ([Rev 20:9](Rev.20.9)).

Jewish traditions vary regarding the locations of **Gog and Magog**. They are symbolically to the north (see [Jer 1:14-15](Jer.1.14-Jer.1.15)), the direction from which the enemies traditionally approached Megiddo and Jerusalem. The names represent nations and rulers from **every corner of the earth** that oppose God’s people (see [Ezek 38–39](Ezek.38.1-Ezek.39.29)).

**He will gather them together for battle:** Repeating the earlier scenes in which God’s enemies assemble for battle ([Rev 16:16](Rev.16.16); [19:19](Rev.19.19)), Satan here makes a last-ditch attempt to confront God and his forces.

Again, no battle occurs (see [16:16-21](Rev.16.16-Rev.16.21); [19:19-21](Rev.19.19-Rev.19.21)), because **fire from heaven came down** *. . .* **and consumed them** as it did Sodom ([Gen 19:24](Gen.19.24); see also [2 Kgs 1:10-12](2Kgs.1.10-2Kgs.1.12); [Ezek 38:22-23](Ezek.38.22-Ezek.38.23); [39:6](Ezek.39.6)). The enemies of God cannot stand against him.

**they will be tormented . . . forever:** Rebellion against God has eternal consequences. While the concept of unending punishment repulses some, it is the message of Revelation and of Scripture generally that God will deal sternly with sin and rebellion by those who reject Christ’s saving work (see [Matt 13:42](Matt.13.42); [25:41-46](Matt.25.41-Matt.25.46); [John 3:18](John.3.18), [36](John.3.36); [Rom 2:7](Rom.2.7)). Perhaps more than any book in Scripture, Revelation illustrates that the unrepentant persist in their rebellion despite the consequences ([Rev 9:20-21](Rev.9.20-Rev.9.21); [16:9-11](Rev.16.9-Rev.16.11); cp. [Luke 16:31](Luke.16.31)). Revelation also emphasizes that God is just and deals with sin as it deserves.
This segment portrays a court hearing at which the dead are judged on the basis of their works. God’s response to eternal rebellion is eternal punishment.
**books were opened:** See [Ps 56:8](Ps.56.8); [Dan 7:10](Dan.7.10).

**The Book of Life** holds the names of faithful people who have experienced God’s saving power ([Mal 3:16](Mal.3.16); see [Rev 3:5](Rev.3.5); [13:8](Rev.13.8); [17:8](Rev.17.8); [20:15](Rev.20.15)); they are probably the same ones as those who experience the “first resurrection” ([20:5-6](Rev.20.5-Rev.20.6)).
**And the dead were judged:** The works of both the redeemed and the unredeemed will be judged (see [22:12](Rev.22.12); [Matt 16:27](Matt.16.27); [25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)).
**the grave:** See study note on 6:7-8.
The expression **death and the grave** refers to the reality of death; it is the last enemy that God will destroy (see [21:4](Rev.21.4); [1 Cor 15:26](1Cor.15.26)).

The **lake of fire** portrays the horrible end of God’s enemies who will not experience the “first resurrection” (see [Rev 20:5-6](Rev.20.5-Rev.20.6); cp. [Matt 25:41](Matt.25.41); [Luke 16:24](Luke.16.24); [Jude 1:7](Jude.1.7)).

The final scenes of the new heaven and earth are striking pictures of a new community and home for God’s people that is fashioned and given by God. These scenes help to lift the spirits of persecuted Christians. John lays out his basic vision ([21:1-8](Rev.21.1-Rev.21.8)) and follows it with two expansions: (1) In [21:9-27](Rev.21.9-Rev.21.27), he presents the new Jerusalem as the site of holy perfection; (2) in [22:1-5](Rev.22.1-Rev.22.5), he describes the new Jerusalem as the ultimate Garden of Eden that Adam and Eve could have experienced had they not sinned.

The vision involves God’s creation of the new **heaven** and **earth** (cp. [Gen 1:1](Gen.1.1) with [Isa 65:17](Isa.65.17); [66:22](Isa.66.22)). The **old** creation has **disappeared**—it was subject to decay (see [Rom 8:20-21](Rom.8.20-Rom.8.21); [2 Pet 3:7](2Pet.3.7), [10](2Pet.3.10)).

**the sea was also gone:** The sea was associated with chaos or the abyss (see study note on Rev 9:1-12) and was sometimes portrayed as a roaring monster (see [Pss 46:3](Ps.46.3); [74:14](Ps.74.14); see also [Job 3:8](Job.3.8); [41:1-34](Job.41.1-Job.41.34); [Luke 21:25](Luke.21.25)). The new creation will be free from all such evil.
**coming down from God:** The new creation is a gift from God. In the beginning, God created everything good, and in the end, God will create a new, unbroken world.

This picture of **Jerusalem** as a beautiful **bride** (see [Isa 61:10](Isa.61.10)) contrasts starkly with the vision of Babylon (or Rome) as the prostitute ([Rev 17:4-5](Rev.17.4-Rev.17.5); [18:2-3](Rev.18.2-Rev.18.3); see study note on 21:9–22:9).

**God’s home is now among his people!** Old and New Testament expectations are fully and finally realized. Ever since humanity sinned ([Gen 3](Gen.3.1-Gen.3.24)), separation from God has been humanity’s greatest problem ([Gen 3:23](Gen.3.23)). God has repeatedly called his people to himself through the prophets, through Jesus his Son, and through the presence of the Spirit (see [Gen 17:8](Gen.17.8); [Exod 29:45-46](Exod.29.45-Exod.29.46); [Pss 46:4-5](Ps.46.4-Ps.46.5); [95:7](Ps.95.7); [Jer 7:23](Jer.7.23); [31:33](Jer.31.33); [Ezek 34:14](Ezek.34.14); [37:27](Ezek.37.27); [Zech 8:8](Zech.8.8); [John 14:2-3](John.14.2-John.14.3); [17:24](John.17.24)). In the new heaven and new earth, God’s people will finally experience ultimate and everlasting fellowship with God.

**no more death or sorrow or crying or pain:** See [Isa 25:8](Isa.25.8); [1 Cor 15:54](1Cor.15.54). God’s people will know the creative wholeness and salvation that Christ brings (see [2 Cor 5:17](2Cor.5.17); [Gal 6:15](Gal.6.15)).
God restates Jesus’ final words from the cross, **It is finished!** ([John 19:30](John.19.30); cp. [Rev 16:17](Rev.16.17)), connecting Christ’s death with the assurance of eternal life.

**I am the Alpha and the Omega:** With the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, John portrays God as encompassing total reality and total truth. God was from the **Beginning** (see [Gen 1:1](Gen.1.1); cp. [John 1:1-2](John.1.1-John.1.2)) and is also the **End** (see [Rev 1:8](Rev.1.8); [22:13](Rev.22.13)).

Because Christ is supreme and in charge of all things (see [Rom 9:5](Rom.9.5); [1 Cor 15:28](1Cor.15.28); [Eph 1:22-23](Eph.1.22-Eph.1.23); [4:5-6](Eph.4.5-Eph.4.6)), he dispenses **the water of life** to all who are **thirsty** for it (see study note on Rev 7:16-17; see also [Isa 55:1](Isa.55.1); [John 4:10](John.4.10); [7:37-38](John.7.37-John.7.38)).

**All who are victorious:** God’s **children** who persevere in life **will inherit** his **blessings**. Adoption is a covenant relationship; the language of adoption certifies their privileges and responsibilities (cp. [Gen 17:8](Gen.17.8); [2 Sam 7:14-16](2Sam.7.14-2Sam.7.16); [Jer 31:33](Jer.31.33); [Ezek 34:24](Ezek.34.24)).

This vice list summarizes sins described throughout Revelation. These sins characterize people who have not experienced adoption by God; their fate is the **fiery lake** (see [Rom 1:29-32](Rom.1.29-Rom.1.32); [Gal 5:19-21](Gal.5.19-Gal.5.21); [2 Tim 3:2-5](2Tim.3.2-2Tim.3.5); cp. [Exod 20:13-17](Exod.20.13-Exod.20.17); see also study note on Rev 20:10).

**all liars:** John apparently viewed deception as the root of sin; elsewhere he describes Satan as the “father of lies” ([John 8:44](John.8.44); [1 Jn 2:4](1John.2.4); see [Rev 14:5](Rev.14.5); [21:27](Rev.21.27); [22:15](Rev.22.15); cp. [Matt 12:34](Matt.12.34)).

This symbolic vision of the new Jerusalem uses vivid word pictures to describe **the bride, the wife of the Lamb**—all those who respond to Christ’s message of salvation (see [21:2](Rev.21.2); [22:17](Rev.22.17); [Eph 5:22-32](Eph.5.22-Eph.5.32)).

**a great, high mountain:** In Scripture, experiences with God frequently take place on the mountains (cp. [Ezek 40:2](Ezek.40.2); see also [Exod 3:1](Exod.3.1); [19:10-25](Exod.19.10-Exod.19.25); [Deut 34:1-4](Deut.34.1-Deut.34.4); [1 Kgs 18:20-40](1Kgs.18.20-1Kgs.18.40); [19:8-18](1Kgs.19.8-1Kgs.19.18); [Matt 5:1](Matt.5.1); [15:29](Matt.15.29); [17:1](Matt.17.1); [24:3](Matt.24.3); [28:16](Matt.28.16)).

**the holy city . . . descending out of heaven from God:** God’s presence and eternal life cannot be reached by human effort but are received as a gift ([Eph 2:8-9](Eph.2.8-Eph.2.9); cp. [2 Cor 5:1](2Cor.5.1)).
Like the true people of God, the **glory** of the city reflects God’s glory (cp. [Exod 34:29-35](Exod.34.29-Exod.34.35); [2 Cor 3:7-11](2Cor.3.7-2Cor.3.11)).

**Jasper** (see also [Rev 4:3](Rev.4.3); [21:11](Rev.21.11), [18](Rev.21.18)) is opaque on earth; the heavenly jasper is **clear as crystal***,* having a transparency that mirrors God’s purity and integrity.

In this vision, **the twelve tribes of Israel** represent the redeemed people of God (see [7:4-8](Rev.7.4-Rev.7.8); see also [Rom 9:6-7](Rom.9.6-Rom.9.7)). The foundation for this community of God’s redeemed is **the twelve apostles of the Lamb**. In Jesus, God’s promise to bless all of the families of the earth through Abraham has been fully realized ([Gen 12:3](Gen.12.3)).
**measure the city:** Measuring defines accepted boundaries (contrast the unmeasured section of the Temple, [11:2](Rev.11.2); see also [Ezek 40:3–42:20](Ezek.40.3-Ezek.42.20)).
The city is described as a perfect cube. Each dimension is **1,400 miles** (Greek *12,000 stadia*); the number *12,000* symbolically represents the people of God (see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note).

In the ancient world, **walls** were important not only to the defense and boundary of a city, but also to its status. That these walls are **216 feet thick** (Greek *144 cubits*) indicates the strength of God’s redeemed people. The measurement of *144 cubits* again uses a multiple of 12 to represent God’s people. A cubit was the length of a man’s forearm, with a standard length of about 18 inches.

The **wall** is built of **jasper** (see study note on 21:11; cp. [4:3](Rev.4.3)). The city is fashioned in **gold***,* which is not opaque like earthly gold; rather, like God’s transformed people, the heavenly gold is **clear** and **pure**.

The **twelve precious stones** adorning the **foundation stones** of the city’s **wall** are a reminder of the twelve stones on the high priests’ breastplate that represented the people of God (see [Exod 28:17-20](Exod.28.17-Exod.28.20)).
Things that are precious and luxurious on earth are common building materials in heaven.

**I saw no temple:** This apparent conflict with earlier visions ([11:19](Rev.11.19); [14:15-17](Rev.14.15-Rev.14.17)) is resolved by understanding each visionary picture in Revelation as a separate symbolic representation of God’s presence. There is no longer any need for a temple in heaven because God is present with his people.

The vitality, energy, and life of the city are not in institutions or physical sources of power and light, but in **the glory of God** and the Lamb. The **sun** and **moon** were features of the first creation ([Gen 1:14-19](Gen.1.14-Gen.1.19); see [Isa 60:19-20](Isa.60.19-Isa.60.20)).
**the Lamb is its light:** Jesus is the light of the world (see [John 8:12](John.8.12); [9:5](John.9.5); [12:35-36](John.12.35-John.12.36)).
**The nations:** God’s promise to Abraham is fulfilled ([Gen 12:3](Gen.12.3); see [Isa 2:3](Isa.2.3)).

In Revelation, **the kings of the world** usually refer to God’s enemies ([Rev 6:15](Rev.6.15); [17:18](Rev.17.18); [18:3](Rev.18.3), [9](Rev.18.9)). Now that the enemies have been destroyed ([16:9](Rev.16.9), [11](Rev.16.11); [19:1-2](Rev.19.1-Rev.19.2), [19-21](Rev.19.19-Rev.19.21)), the picture is of God’s **glory** as reflected in those people who have repented ([14:6-7](Rev.14.6-Rev.14.7); cp. [11:13](Rev.11.13)) and walk with God ([5:9](Rev.5.9); [15:4](Rev.15.4)).

The **gates** that are **never** . . . **closed** contrast with the ancient scene in which closed gates protected cities from enemies, particularly at night. The people enjoy peace and security in God’s supremacy (see [Isa 60:11](Isa.60.11)). God’s enemies have been destroyed, and fear and failure have ended (see [Zech 14:7](Zech.14.7); [John 11:8-10](John.11.8-John.11.10); [12:35-36](John.12.35-John.12.36)).

**evil** (or *ceremonially unclean*): Spiritual impurity is a basic concern in Revelation (see [21:8](Rev.21.8)). Evil is here generalized as **idolatry and dishonesty** (see [Rev 14:5](Rev.14.5); [21:8](Rev.21.8); [22:15](Rev.22.15)). Those who fail to appear in the **Book of Life** are excluded from the city of God. Only those **whose names are written** in the Book of Life, the pure of heart ([Matt 5:8](Matt.5.8)), will see God.

This part of John’s vision of the city deals with God’s provision of water and food for his people (cp. [Exod 16:4](Exod.16.4), [22-24](Exod.16.22-Exod.16.24); [Ezek 47:1-12](Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.12); [John 4:10](John.4.10); [6:32-35](John.6.32-John.6.35)). Although God originally made a “garden of delight” (Eden) for Adam and Eve, they disobeyed him and lost it ([Gen 2–3](Gen.2.1-Gen.3.24)). Now Eden is refashioned and united to the celestial city as God’s marvelous gift for his faithful people.

Although humans were denied access to the **tree of life** after they sinned (see [Gen 3:22-24](Gen.3.22-Gen.3.24)), it is now freely available. The tree **on each side of the river** (cp. [Ezek 47:12](Ezek.47.12)) shows that there is no wrong side of the river in heaven. The tree produces **a fresh crop** of fruit **each month***,* demonstrating God’s constant provision.

**No longer . . . a curse:** Ever since the first sin ([Gen 3:14-19](Gen.3.14-Gen.3.19)), humanity has been cursed because of their rebellion against God (see [1 Cor 16:22](1Cor.16.22)). Now rebellion, sin, and the curse are gone forever.
**his servants will worship him:** Revelation gives glimpses of authentic worship (see [Rev 4–5](Rev.4.1-Rev.5.14); [7:9-17](Rev.7.9-Rev.7.17)).

The human fears of death and of seeing God (see [Gen 16:13](Gen.16.13); [32:30](Gen.32.30); [Judg 6:22](Judg.6.22); [Isa 6:5](Isa.6.5)) will be removed. God’s people will bear his name and **will see his face** with joy (see [Matt 5:8](Matt.5.8); [2 Cor 3:18](2Cor.3.18); [1 Jn 3:2-3](1John.3.2-1John.3.3)).

**They will reign** with God **forever** (see [20:4](Rev.20.4); see also [5:10](Rev.5.10)) in his radiant light that banishes **night** and the **need for lamps** (see [Isa 60:19-20](Isa.60.19-Isa.60.20)).

This epilogue to Revelation contains utterances by an angel ([22:6](Rev.22.6), [8-11](Rev.22.8-Rev.22.11)) and Christ ([22:7](Rev.22.7), [12-19](Rev.22.12-Rev.22.19)) followed by a concluding plea for Christ’s return ([22:20](Rev.22.20)) and a closing benediction ([22:21](Rev.22.21)). The epilogue has a number of direct verbal connections with the introduction to the book ([1:1-11](Rev.1.1-Rev.1.11)), and it sums up important themes such as encouraging faithful perseverance, warning evildoers, affirming the authenticity of the prophetic message, and restating the nearness of Christ’s return.

**Everything** that John records in Revelation is **trustworthy and true** because **God***,* who has all authority (cp. [Matt 28:18](Matt.28.18)), **has sent** the messenger. But it does not mean these visions are easy to understand.

**Blessed:** The sixth blessing of Revelation (see [1:3](Rev.1.3); [14:13](Rev.14.13); [16:15](Rev.16.15); [19:9](Rev.19.9); [20:6](Rev.20.6); [22:14](Rev.22.14)) is for **those who obey**. Obedience is key to God’s blessing.

The earlier warning against false worship (see [19:10](Rev.19.10)) is reiterated when John again falls **at the feet of the angel**. **Only God** deserves our **worship** (cp. John the Baptist in relation to Jesus; [John 1:6-8](John.1.6-John.1.8), [26-27](John.1.26-John.1.27); [3:27-35](John.3.27-John.3.35)).

**Do not seal up:** The angel expands John’s initial instruction to “write in a book” ([1:11](Rev.1.11)) and warns against curtailing its communication. Although some things are sealed—God does not reveal everything (cp. [10:4](Rev.10.4))—what has been written must be communicated so that people will understand the seriousness of the message and that **the time is near** (see [1:1](Rev.1.1), [3](Rev.1.3); [22:6-7](Rev.22.6-Rev.22.7); cp. [Dan 12:4](Dan.12.4)).

**Vile** people who refuse to accept God’s forgiveness will **continue to be vile** (see [16:9](Rev.16.9)), yet John reminds the **righteous** to maintain their integrity. This verse is a warning to evildoers, and it calls the righteous to recognize the crucial significance of Christ’s return relative to their commitments and their actions.

Christ is **coming soon** *. . .* **to repay all people***,* not just on the basis of their profession of faith, but **according to their deeds** (see [2:23](Rev.2.23); [11:18](Rev.11.18); [14:13](Rev.14.13); [20:12-13](Rev.20.12-Rev.20.13); see also [Prov 24:12](Prov.24.12); [Matt 16:27](Matt.16.27); [2 Cor 5:10](2Cor.5.10)). Not every statement of belief is genuine ([John 2:23-25](John.2.23-John.2.25)); faith will show itself in actions ([Jas 2:14-26](Jas.2.14-Jas.2.26)). We are indeed saved by the grace and power of God in Christ. Our works do not save us, but they do indicate the seriousness of our confession and provide a just basis for our ultimate reward or punishment.

**Blessed are those:** In response to the connection between actions and ultimate results ([22:12](Rev.22.12)), the seventh blessing of Revelation (see also [1:3](Rev.1.3); [14:13](Rev.14.13); [16:15](Rev.16.15); [19:9](Rev.19.9); [20:6](Rev.20.6); [22:7](Rev.22.7)) promises acceptance for **those who wash their robes**—those who have been purified by trusting in Christ and following him faithfully ([3:5](Rev.3.5); [6:11](Rev.6.11); [7:9-10](Rev.7.9-Rev.7.10), [14](Rev.7.14); [19:13](Rev.19.13); [Eph 5:26](Eph.5.26); [Heb 10:22](Heb.10.22)).
**enter through the gates of the city:** See study note on Rev 21:24-25.

This verse again lists those who are not admitted to contrast with those admitted in [22:14](Rev.22.14) (see [21:8](Rev.21.8), [27](Rev.21.27); [22:11](Rev.22.11)). These unrepentant sinners remain **outside the city***;* it is another warning to those who do not repent that they will not be allowed to enter the city of God ([22:14](Rev.22.14)).

The reference to sinners as **dogs** was a familiar Jewish designation for rejected outsiders (see [Matt 7:6](Matt.7.6); [Phil 3:2](Phil.3.2); also [2 Sam 3:8](2Sam.3.8); [2 Kgs 8:13](2Kgs.8.13)); Jews used this term to refer to Gentiles (see [Mark 7:26-28](Mark.7.26-Mark.7.28)).

**I am both the source of David and the heir to his throne: Jesus** validates the **message** of Revelation (cp. [John 21:24](John.21.24)) by swearing that he is simultaneously *the source of David* (see [Rev 5:5](Rev.5.5); [Isa 11:10](Isa.11.10)) and David’s *heir* (see [Ezek 37:23-24](Ezek.37.23-Ezek.37.24); [Rom 1:3](Rom.1.3)).
The **morning star** was a name for the Messiah (see [Num 24:17](Num.24.17); [2 Pet 1:19](2Pet.1.19); cp. [Luke 1:78-79](Luke.1.78-Luke.1.79)).
**Come** is a repeated invitation and a confession (see [22:20](Rev.22.20)).
**the bride:** The Lamb’s wife (see [21:9](Rev.21.9)) is the church, the people of God.
The **thirsty** can **drink freely** from God’s provision (see [21:6](Rev.21.6); [22:1](Rev.22.1); [Ps 42:1](Ps.42.1); [Isa 55:1](Isa.55.1); [John 4:10-14](John.4.10-John.4.14)).

**I solemnly declare:** John issues an oath to protect the integrity of the book of Revelation. He declares a curse upon anyone who alters the contents of the book or its message (cp. [Deut 4:2](Deut.4.2); [12:32](Deut.12.32)). The curse contrasts with the statement of blessing on all who read aloud, listen to, and obey the prophecy ([Rev 1:3](Rev.1.3)). At the time Revelation was written, scribes would sometimes alter books to suit their own views. Early Christians quickly developed means of authenticating both messages and messengers (see [John 21:24](John.21.24); [1 Cor 16:21](1Cor.16.21); [Gal 6:11](Gal.6.11); [Col 4:18](Col.4.18); [2 Thes 3:17](2Thess.3.17); [1 Jn 4:1-3](1John.4.1-1John.4.3)).

Since the time of the early church, the scope and content of the New Testament has been established as the measure of the Christian proclamation. Yet the church continues to be plagued by those who would attempt to reconstruct the borders of Scripture by adding other works that they believe are of equal status with the Bible or by arguing that certain segments of the Bible are unreliable creations of human effort and perception. The genuine church has rejected and will continue to reject efforts to redefine the boundaries of the canon as human and even demonic attempts to alter the basis of the Christian faith.
**I am coming soon!** See [3:11](Rev.3.11).
**Come, Lord Jesus!** Paul uttered the same response ([1 Cor 16:22](1Cor.16.22); see also [Phil 4:5](Phil.4.5)).
Revelation closes with a benediction similar to those in Paul’s letters (e.g., [Rom 15:33](Rom.15.33); [1 Cor 16:23-24](1Cor.16.23-1Cor.16.24)).
The fitting final sentence invokes **the grace of the Lord Jesus***,* the foundation of our forgiveness and the basis of our eternal hope.
